entries.answer: Happy names an emotional state but has drifted a long way from it, now also meaning pleased about a circumstance, as in a happy solution, or willing, as in I would be happy to help. The drift has all been towards the agreeable, so the word now covers anything at all the speaker is glad about. It also fits a moment better than a person, since anyone can be happy about a thing without being what anyone would call a happy person.

entries.answer: Sad covers an enormous range, from downcast to genuinely grieving, and English does not mark the difference the way some languages do with separate terms for sorrow and for disappointment. It also does service outside emotion, so a sad song and a sad failure are both ordinary. The noun sadness is the formal one and the everyday form is being sad, which is what people actually say, and the difference is one of register rather than meaning.

entries.answer: Angry names a state that English splits by cause rather than by degree, so frustrated, irritated, annoyed, livid and furious are all separate words rather than degrees of one. Choosing correctly is therefore a matter of reading the situation rather than of reaching for the strongest term available. The word also applies to something inanimate, as in an angry sky, which is a poetic extension rather than a mistake.

entries.answer: Anxious names a state of worry about something uncertain, and the word has widened considerably, so anxious about a result and anxious to meet them are both ordinary. It sits between nervous and afraid, nearer nervous when the thing is expected and nearer afraid when it is not. In medical use anxiety also names a condition, and a condition is not the same thing as the ordinary feeling of it.

entries.answer: Grateful is the plain adjective for thankfulness, and English offers a small set of near-synonyms in being thankful, appreciative and obliged, each at a slightly different register. Grateful is the commonest, while appreciative tends to be used when the thing thanked is an experience rather than a person, as in appreciative of the feedback. Obliged is the oldest and the most formal, and it survives mainly in British official writing.

entries.answer: Embarrassed names the feeling of being personally exposed, and what separates it from ashamed is the target, since embarrassment is about how others see the situation while shame is about your own judgement of yourself. That is why a compliment can embarrass without shaming, and why the two words are not interchangeable. The noun embarrassment is the formal one, while the everyday phrase is feeling embarrassed, and the difference between them is register alone.
